metadata.title: Towards the implementation of automated scoring in international large-scale assessments: Scalability and quality control

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2023 constructed-response (CR) item responses across participating countries, but it does not report the use of TIMSS sampling/survey weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation. The analytic workflow instead focuses on training/test splitting (80:20) of human-scored responses and evaluating automated scoring agreement metrics (EA and Cohen’s kappa) on the held-out test set. Because the paper does not specify weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or complex-survey handling, readers should treat the reported agreement statistics as conditional on the sampled response sets rather than as population-representative estimates. For operational use, analysts should consider whether TIMSS complex sampling weights are needed for country-level generalization, especially if extending beyond the scored response subsets.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not model cognitive achievement scores with TIMSS plausible values; instead, it dichotomously scores constructed responses (correct=1/incorrect=0) using automated scoring methods. Missing-data handling is therefore not described in the PV sense; the paper instead applies explicit filtering rules (e.g., excluding aberrant responses and removing responses that cannot be translated). The absence of a formal missing-data strategy for other potential missingness (e.g., incomplete translations or preprocessing failures) is a reporting gap for transparency, though the main exclusions are documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses three TIMSS 2023 science CR items: Item 1 (Grade 4 Physical Science), Item 2 (Grade 4 Life Science), and Item 3 (Grade 8 Physics). Aberrant responses consisting solely of punctuation, numbers, single characters, or repetitive characters were automatically machine-scored as 0 and excluded from the automated scoring training and validation process. For supervised learning, the remaining responses were split into training and test sets using an 80:20 ratio across all countries. For machine translation, responses were removed from training/test if they were identified as untranslated (e.g., Google Translate returning original-language text or non-dictionary transliterations; ChatGPT outputting 'uncertain' after re-translation).

main_findings.target_variable: Automated scoring correctness (human vs machine agreement)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best method: MMT_ANNs. Untranslated responses: 0.79% (MMT_ANNs) vs 2.64% (Google_ANNs), 1.15% (ChatGPT_ANNs), 1.97% (Unsupervised Learning). Agreement on test set: EA=92.49%, Cohen’s kappa=0.83 (MMT_ANNs) vs EA=91.52%/κ=0.81 (Google_ANNs), EA=89.45%/κ=0.77 (ChatGPT_ANNs), EA=91.54%/κ=0.81 (UL).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 4 Physical Science (Item 1 CR) the study leveraged multilingual machine translation combined with a feed-forward neural network (MMT_ANNs) to predict whether each constructed response matched the human correct/incorrect score, finding that MMT_ANNs achieved the highest human-machine agreement (EA=92.49%, κ=0.83) with the lowest untranslated rate (0.79%) on the test set. This indicates that scalable multilingual automated scoring can serve as a reliable quality-control layer for CR items across countries, reducing reliance on second human raters while maintaining high scoring consistency, though it may still be sensitive to translation errors for heavily misspelled or low-resource-language responses.

main_findings.target_variable: Automated scoring correctness (human vs machine agreement)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best method: MMT_ANNs. Untranslated responses: 0.51% (MMT_ANNs) vs 1.74% (Google_ANNs), 0.87% (ChatGPT_ANNs), 1.53% (Unsupervised Learning). Agreement on test set: EA=94.19%, Cohen’s kappa=0.87 (MMT_ANNs) vs EA=93.69%/κ=0.86 (Google_ANNs), EA=91.34%/κ=0.81 (ChatGPT_ANNs), EA=89.64%/κ=0.77 (UL).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 4 Life Science (Item 2 CR) the study leveraged multilingual machine translation combined with a feed-forward neural network (MMT_ANNs) to predict whether each constructed response matched the human correct/incorrect score, finding that MMT_ANNs produced the strongest agreement with human raters (EA=94.19%, κ=0.87) and the lowest untranslated rate (0.51%) on the test set. This indicates that multilingual automated scoring can be implemented consistently for CR items in ILSAs, supporting scalable scoring validation across participating countries, while highlighting that performance depends on translation quality and may vary for specific country-language groups.

main_findings.target_variable: Automated scoring correctness (human vs machine agreement)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best method: MMT_ANNs. Untranslated responses: 1.13% (MMT_ANNs) vs 2.52% (Google_ANNs), 2.16% (ChatGPT_ANNs), 0.96% (Unsupervised Learning). Agreement on test set: EA=94.88%, Cohen’s kappa=0.87 (MMT_ANNs) vs EA=93.65%/κ=0.85 (Google_ANNs), EA=91.61%/κ=0.80 (ChatGPT_ANNs), EA=91.95%/κ=0.81 (UL).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 8 Physics (Item 3 CR) the study leveraged multilingual machine translation combined with a feed-forward neural network (MMT_ANNs) to predict whether each constructed response matched the human correct/incorrect score, finding that MMT_ANNs achieved the highest agreement with human scoring (EA=94.88%, κ=0.87) on the test set. This indicates that automated scoring can be extended to higher-grade science CR items across many languages as a scalable quality-control mechanism, though misalignment can still occur due to human rater strictness and translation failures (e.g., hallucinations or polysemy) in certain country-language groups.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates automated scoring for three TIMSS 2023 science constructed-response items (Grade 4 Physical Science, Grade 4 Life Science, and Grade 8 Physics) across participating countries and 42 languages. Responses were dichotomously scored (correct=1/incorrect=0) and filtered to exclude aberrant responses and untranslated outputs; the remaining data were split 80:20 into training and test sets. The best-performing approach was MMT_ANNs, which combine Google Translate and ChatGPT-based translation with a feed-forward neural network trained on bag-of-words features. On the test set, MMT_ANNs achieved the highest agreement with human scoring across items, with average EA and Cohen’s kappa of 93.85% and 0.86, respectively, and the lowest standardized mean score differences (SMD) (average SMD=0). Limitations include reliance on bag-of-words (ignoring word order/context), sensitivity to translation quality for misspellings and low-resource languages, and lack of reported complex-survey weighting or a formal missing-data strategy beyond explicit exclusions.
